transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we dive in, I want to flag a critical privacy and clinical regulatory finding from a working session I held yesterday with the product lead and privacy office. We confirmed that the company's non-negotiable position on clinical data is that any publication of project results must prohibit patient-level data entirely, and de-identification must be required before any permitted external publication. This directly bears on the current draft, which permits publication of project results without those constraints. I'll formally state my required actions for the record: the publication clause must be revised to explicitly prohibit patient-level data and mandate de-identification before any external publication. I'd like to get this on the table early so we can discuss how it interacts with the IP and licensing terms.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: Thank you, Nadia. That's a clear and well-supported finding. The publication constraints you've described — prohibiting patient-level data and mandating de-identification before external publication — are consistent with protecting both our regulatory posture and our commercial interests, especially given that the current draft grants the university an exclusive commercial license to all background technology. Before I can formally approve this agreement, company policy requires a recorded readout from both you as Privacy and Clinical Regulatory Counsel and from our Intellectual Property Counsel. Your required actions are now on the record. I'd like to hear from IP Counsel next on the licensing and background technology terms, and specifically how the publication rights in the current draft interact with the exclusive license grant. Once both readouts are complete, I can move to conditional approval with written revision commitments to be finalized before execution.

transcript.text: I need to put a critical IP finding on the record. I reviewed the university's master research agreement and the controlling schedule they supplied overnight. I confirmed that background patents U1, U2, and U3 are licensed to the company only for noncommercial academic use. The current draft grants the university an exclusive commercial license to all background technology, which would improperly sweep these three patents into a commercial license grant that exceeds the scope of our existing rights. My required actions for the record are: the final agreement must explicitly exclude patents U1, U2, and U3 from any commercial license grant, and must require separate written university consent before any commercial use of those patents. I have not yet incorporated this into the draft or circulated the finding, as the schedule only came in overnight.
